The initiative would grant a supplement to retired persons in the amount of one-twelfth of their annual pension. This would have the consequence that the old-age pensions under the OASI would be calculated in a first step without the supplement, so that the amount of possible pensions whose calculation is based on the old-age pension can be determined. Only in a second step would the supplement be added once a year to the old-age pension and exclusively to this (p. 8).

Recipients of disability pensions or survivors' pensions, on the other hand, would not be taken into account, which would lead to unequal treatment of the insured under the 1st pillar (p. 10).

According to Annex 3 of the dispatch, an additional old-age pension from the Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance (AHV) or an increase in pensions by 8.33 percent would increase the AHV's expenditure in 2032 by around 5 billion francs. Since the higher AHV expenditure would also lead to an increase in the federal contribution and thus the AHV's revenue by around 1 billion francs, the financial result would not deteriorate by the same amount, but by almost 4 billion francs.

The initiative committee justifies the necessity of a surcharge on the AHV old-age pensions by stating that the current amount of the AHV old-age pensions is too small for low to medium income classes to guarantee adequate financial security for pensioners when transitioning into retirement. They point out that half of all individuals who retired in 2018 had to make do with less than 1,772 francs in AHV pension per month. Furthermore, it is argued that for a significant part of the population, particularly women, this income is not or only marginally supplemented by the pension fund.

The dispatch notes that a supplement for AHV old-age pensioners would also be problematic from the point of view of generational fairness. Because today's and future gainfully employed individuals would have to bear an increasingly higher burden over time, just to ensure the previous level of benefits. These burdens are also higher than those which the majority of today's pensioners had to bear during their gainful employment (p. 19).

The Federal Council predicts that the additional expenditure for the old-age and survivors' insurance (AHV) would amount to around 5 billion francs in the year 2032 if the initiative is accepted (p. 11).

The initiators propose that the additional expenditure for the surcharge could be financed by increasing the wage contributions of employees and employers or by using part of the profits of the National Bank. (p. 5)

The initiative meets the requirements for validity under Article 139, paragraph 3 of the Federal Constitution: 
a. It is formulated as a fully elaborated draft and thus meets the requirements for unity of form. 
b. There is a material connection between the individual parts of the initiative. The initiative thus meets the requirements for unity of matter. 
c. The initiative does not violate any mandatory provisions of international law. It thus meets the requirements for compatibility with international law.

The popular initiative "For a better life in old age (Initiative for a 13th AHV pension)" was submitted on 28 May 2021 with the necessary number of valid signatures. By decision of 22 June 2021, the Federal Chancellery established that the initiative had been successful with 101,793 valid signatures.

(p. 3)
According to page 16, in the year 2019, 26 percent of the OASI pension recipients (excluding benefit-receiving partners) received a maximum pension.

(p. 3) The Federal Council requests the federal chambers to recommend the popular initiative "For a better life in old age (Initiative for a 13th AHV pension)" to the people and the cantons for rejection without a direct counter-proposal and without an indirect counter-proposal.

(p. 4-5) Although the initiative would increase the AHV replacement rate once again, the effect of the declining AHV replacement rate is relativized in the overall consideration of the 1st and 2nd pillars: Since occupational pension provision as the 2nd pillar builds on the benefits of the AHV, not the entire income is insured in this case, but rather a so-called coordination deduction is made.

(p. 5) The Federal Council also argues that the initiative would lead to an additional burden for those paying contributions and that the financing of the increased expenditure is not secured.

(p. 20-21) Furthermore, acceptance of the initiative would increase the deficit in the AHV, which would represent an additional risk to the financial stability of the AHV.

(p. 22-23) The Federal Council's reasoning is therefore not focused on solving the problems with the declining AHV replacement rate, but rather on the fact that the initiative would lead to a disproportionate burden for those paying contributions and for the Confederation.

The question cannot be answered because in the dispatch of the Federal Council no explanation can be found as to why the initiative would create unequal treatment of the 1st pillar. The Federal Council merely requests that the initiative be rejected, without explicitly referring to this criticism.

According to Annex 3 of the dispatch, the revenue deficit in the AHV would amount to around 8.7 billion francs in 2032 if the initiative is accepted. The federal contribution would increase by around 913 million francs (cf. Annex 5).

(p. 6) The initiators place the initiative in a context with the 2nd pillar of old-age provision, occupational pension provision according to the Federal Act of June 25, 1982, on Occupational Old-Age, Survivors', and Disability Pension Provision (BVG). People with low incomes from their gainful employment are, in the opinion of the initiative committee, more dependent on the AHV because they often have poorer coverage in the 2nd pillar and can save less pension capital.

(p. 7) The smaller endowment with pension capital from occupational pension provision thus increases the importance of AHV pensions for these individuals. For this reason, a supplement to the AHV old-age pensions is justified.

(p. 8) An annual supplement in the amount of one-twelfth of the AHV old-age pension would change the total amount of pensions paid out per year. However, the dynamics of the development of pensions and wages would remain intact.

(p. 9) The initiative provides for a supplement only for old-age pensioners. Recipients of IV or survivors' pensions, on the other hand, would not be taken into account. However, the Federal Constitution places old-age, survivors', and disability insurance as insurances of the 1st pillar on an equal footing (Art. 111 and 112 BV). An additional payment only of the old-age pension would create a new unequal treatment of the insured persons of the 1st pillar that did not previously exist.

(p. 10) By not including the supplement in the calculation of supplementary benefits, recipients of supplementary benefits to AHV old-age pensions would be better off than other recipients of supplementary benefits.

(p. 11) The effects of the initiative on individual population groups and on the national economy also depend on the financing of the additional expenditures. This is not specified in the initiative.

(p. 12) An additional AHV old-age pension or an increase in pensions by 8.33 percent would increase the expenditures of the AHV in 2032 by around 5 billion francs.

(p. 13) The initiative would also contribute to slowing down the constant decline in the replacement rate due to the pension index. However, acceptance of the initiative would, in particular, assume that the financing of the additional costs is ensured or financially sustainable.

(p. 14) The supplement to the AHV pensions would also be hardly or not at all socially justified for pensioners with higher incomes.

The initiative would therefore actually have a positive effect on pensioners with low incomes, as it provides for an increase in the AHV pension by 8.33 percent. This could contribute to these individuals being financially better off and their existence being more secure.

However, it is to be noted that the financing of the initiative is not specified and acceptance of the initiative would also have effects on the federal finances.

The termination of the FZA would, due to the guillotine clause (Art. 25 para. 4 FZA), lead to the elimination of the Bilaterals I. Through the guillotine clause, six months after notification, all agreements of the Bilaterals I affected by this clause automatically cease to apply.

The Federal Council assumes that a repeal of the FZA and the introduction of a more administered immigration regime with a quantitative limitation on immigration would significantly reduce the growth potential of the Swiss economy. It also mentions that such a repeal would create additional challenges in connection with demographic change.

Furthermore, it is mentioned that the adoption of the initiative would result in a fundamental reorientation of Swiss migration and admission policy with far-reaching consequences. The Federal Council is aware that high immigration and the associated population growth pose challenges.

The Federal Council also mentions that a repeal of the FZA would lead to an increase in complexity and uncertainty in cross-border goods traffic. This could have a negative impact, particularly on companies that are heavily dependent on efficient supply chains.

Overall, the Federal Council assesses the effects of a repeal of the Schengen and Dublin association agreements as negative for the Swiss economy.

The Federal Council assesses the existing strategies and measures as effective in meeting the challenges of immigration. It assumes that a repeal of the FZA and the introduction of a more administered immigration regime with a quantitative limitation on immigration would significantly reduce the growth potential of the Swiss economy. The Federal Council is committed to the proven migration policy and humanitarian principles and wants to reduce immigration, where it is legally possible and politically indicated, with suitable measures.

The Federal Council rejects the popular initiative "No 10 million Switzerland! (Sustainability Initiative)" because it would result in a fundamental reorientation of Swiss migration policy and relations between Switzerland and the EU with far-reaching consequences. The initiative demands the cancellation of the FZA (Free Movement Agreement) between Switzerland and the EU if the permanent resident population of Switzerland exceeds the ten million threshold for the first time before or after the year 2050. The Federal Council is aware that high immigration and the associated population growth pose challenges, but it adheres to the proven migration policy and humanitarian principles. It is of the opinion that a cancellation of the FZA, the elimination of further bilateral agreements with the EU, as well as the cancellation of other international agreements would have severe financial, economic, and social consequences. The Federal Council wants to stabilise and further develop the bilateral path with the EU and assumes that a rigid population upper limit in the Constitution would strongly restrict the necessary flexibility for mastering future challenges.

According to the dispatch, immigration to Switzerland is strongly influenced by economic development. The favourable economic development after the Second World War triggered a strong demand for foreign workers, particularly from Italy. These found employment mainly in seasonal sectors such as agriculture and construction as well as in industry. Despite the economic recession in the mid-1970s and cantonal quotas for annual residents and seasonal workers, the foreign population continued to grow over the years.

The immigration of gainfully employed foreigners rose between 1960 and 1974 to an average of 108,000 persons per year. Between 1975 and 2001, the immigration of gainfully employed foreigners (permanent resident population) was 37,900 persons per year, as well as 110,000 seasonal workers.

The immigration of EU/EFTA nationals increased after the introduction of the FZA in 2002, particularly in the years 2008 and 2013. The migration balance of the permanent foreign resident population between 2002 and 2024 consists of EU/EFTA nationals (62%) and third-country nationals (38%).

Immigration in the asylum sector has been strongly influenced by international crises in recent years. The development of asylum applications in Switzerland largely corresponded to developments at the European level. In 2024, 27,740 asylum applications were filed in Switzerland, which represents a decline of 8.2 percent compared to 2023.

Immigration affects various policy areas such as spatial planning, transport infrastructure, and energy and environmental policy. The Federal Council has developed strategies and measures to address the challenges of immigration.

The adoption of the initiative would, according to the dispatch, lead to a jeopardisation of the Schengen and Dublin association agreements. The Federal Council assumes that the EU would also call into question further agreements with Switzerland that it considers to be connected to the FZA.

The popular initiative "Keine 10-Millionen-Schweiz! (Nachhaltigkeitsinitiative)" [No 10-million Switzerland! (Sustainability Initiative)] provides that the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons with the EU (AFMP) must be terminated if the permanent resident population of Switzerland exceeds the ten million threshold for two years and no exception or safeguard clauses could be negotiated or invoked that would make it possible to comply with the ten million threshold.

The assertion of the Federal Council that the popular initiative 'Keine 10-Millionen-Schweiz' would jeopardize prosperity is not directly justified by the immigration statistics from the EU area. The Federal Council argues, however, also with the necessity of a flexible migration policy in order to be able to react to future challenges. It emphasizes that a rigid population upper limit in the BV would strongly restrict the necessary flexibility for mastering future challenges.

It is, however, important to note that the initiative 'Keine 10-Millionen-Schweiz' also provides for the cancellation of the FZA and thus a disappearance of the free movement of persons with the EU. The Federal Council argues that this would have significant financial, economic, and social consequences.

In total, one can say that the assertion of the Federal Council that the initiative would jeopardize prosperity is not directly justified by the immigration statistics from the EU area. The Federal Council argues, however, also with the necessity of a flexible migration policy and the significant consequences of a disappearance of the free movement of persons with the EU.

The initiative "Keine 10-Millionen-Schweiz!" (Sustainability Initiative) demands a limitation of the permanent resident population to a maximum of ten million. However, the Federal Council is of the opinion that the adoption of this initiative would lead to a fundamental reorientation of Swiss migration and admission policy with far-reaching consequences.

The Federal Council assumes that the abolition of the Free Movement Agreement (FZA) between Switzerland and the EU would have significant financial, economic, and social consequences. The adoption of the initiative would also strongly restrict the necessary flexibility for addressing future challenges.

Instead, the Federal Council has developed strategies and measures to reduce immigration and address the challenges of immigration. In the area of asylum, various measures are to be examined and developed to reduce asylum applications and accelerate asylum procedures.

In the labour market, the potential of well-qualified persons in family reunification is to be better exploited. The FDJP was commissioned to implement a programme that supports the recognition of professional qualifications (diploma recognition) and professional integration in a targeted and effective manner.

In the housing sector, the Fund for the Promotion of Non-Profit Housing Construction (Fonds de roulement) is to be increased by a total of 150 million francs over five years from 2030. Furthermore, adjustments are to be made to the "Lex Koller" (BewG) to tighten the conditions for the acquisition of land by foreign nationals.

The Federal Council has also developed strategies and measures in the areas of education, social insurance, spatial planning, housing, transport infrastructure, energy policy, environmental and health policy, as well as agriculture.

Overall, the Federal Council assumes that the adoption of the initiative "Keine 10-Millionen-Schweiz!" (Sustainability Initiative) would lead to a fundamental reorientation of Swiss migration and admission policy with far-reaching consequences. Instead, the Federal Council has developed strategies and measures to reduce immigration and address the challenges of immigration.

The shortage of housing is a problem that could be limited by restricting the population to ten million. However, the Federal Council has developed plans to solve this problem, such as increasing the Fund for the Promotion of Non-Profit Housing Construction (Fonds de roulement) and adjusting the "Lex Koller" (BewG).

The dispatch describes the difference as follows: "With the adoption of the initiative, the previously necessary and important scope for preserving interests and flexibility in applying neutrality would be largely lost." (p. 23)

In this context, it is mentioned that current neutrality practice allows for a flexible handling of neutrality to preserve national interests with the instrument of neutrality as well as possible. The initiative, however, would restrict this flexibility and anchor neutrality as a principle of foreign policy, which means that any substantial adjustment in the future would require a revision of the constitution (p. 23).

According to the dispatch (p. 22), the good offices play an important role in maintaining Switzerland's neutrality. They form a substantial part of the neutrality policy and enable an active peace contribution. Switzerland can use its neutrality as a mediator to prevent or resolve conflicts.

In the initiative (p. 13), however, the role of the good offices is not explicitly mentioned. The initiative text restricts itself to establishing rules for neutrality and its exercise, without making a connection to the role of Switzerland as a mediator.

The dispatch, on the other hand, emphasizes that the good offices are not only an instrument of neutrality policy but also an important aspect of Switzerland's foreign policy. They enable Switzerland to make an active contribution to peacekeeping and fulfill its role as a mediator.

Overall, it can be said that the initiative provides a narrower definition of neutrality, while the dispatch emphasizes that neutrality is a flexible instrument that must be adapted to the respective circumstances.

The dispatch assesses the effects of the neutrality initiative on Switzerland's sanctions policy as negative. It argues that the prohibition to adopt certain sanctions would strongly restrict the scope for action of Switzerland (p. 25). This could lead to Switzerland no longer being able or only optimally able to safeguard its own short- and long-term economic interests and its reputation as a credible advocate of an international order (p. 26).

The dispatch also emphasizes that the initiative would call into question the support of internationally broadly supported sanctions, which is in the interest of Switzerland, since it is a target article of the Federal Constitution (p. 25). The dispatch also quotes the Foreign Policy Strategy 2024-2027, in which Switzerland as a neutral state wants to assume European co-responsibility.

Overall, the dispatch assesses the effects of the neutrality initiative on Switzerland's sanctions policy as negative and argues that it would lead to a restriction of the scope for action of Switzerland.

The Federal Council recommends the rejection of the popular initiative "Wahrung der schweizerischen Neutralität" because it would lead to a clear change of course in Swiss neutrality, which would have negative effects on the security, economic and foreign policy of Switzerland. The initiative would anchor a rigid understanding of neutrality in the federal constitution, which would lead to less flexibility, numerous issues of interpretation and uncertainties (p. 12). The Federal Council considers the neutrality practice proven over 175 years to be secure and should not be changed (p. 29).

The current legal anchoring of neutrality in Switzerland is described in section 2.2 of the dispatch.

According to Article 173 paragraph 1 letter a and 185 paragraph 1 of the Federal Constitution (BV), the BV states that the Federal Council and the Federal Assembly shall take "measures to preserve [...] the neutrality of Switzerland". However, the BV does not express itself further on the question of what the neutrality of Switzerland is.

Several federal laws refer explicitly or implicitly to neutrality without defining it in terms of content (e.g. Art. 1 of the Federal Act of 27 September 2013 on private security services provided abroad and Art. 83 of the Federal Court Act of 17 June 2005).

Furthermore, it is mentioned that international law recognises and regulates the neutrality of Switzerland under international law. The first official declaration of neutrality was proclaimed by the Old Confederacy at the Tagsatzung of 1674. The invasion of French troops into Switzerland in 1798 led to the end of the Old Confederacy and the neutrality practised until then.

The international legal anchoring of neutrality is described as part of customary international law and the UN Charter. Switzerland has acceded to the Hague Conventions of 1907, which codify the law of neutrality. The law of neutrality regulates the following rights and obligations between the neutral party and the parties to the conflict: rights (inviolability of one's own territory, self-defence, free economic traffic) and obligations (prohibition of military support in armed conflict, prohibition of delivery of war-relevant goods from state-owned stocks).

Overall, the current legal anchoring of neutrality in Switzerland is described as a mixture of federal constitution and international law provisions.
The Federal Chancellery established that the initiative was successful with 129'806 valid signatures. (p. 4)
The Federal Council decided in 2002 that Switzerland, upon its accession to the UN, would enshrine its parallel obligations under neutrality law and the UN Charter. (p. 8)

According to Art. 54a para. 2 E-BV of the initiative text, Switzerland may only permit cooperation with military or defence alliances if a direct military attack on Switzerland or actions preparing such an attack are present.

According to the dispatch of the Federal Council, the adoption of the initiative would lead to a significant restriction of Switzerland's security policy cooperation. The Federal Council argues that the initiative would mean a ban on joining military and defence alliances without a duty to provide assistance, as well as a restriction of security policy cooperation with these alliances (p. 23). This would have the consequence that Switzerland could no longer participate in NATO cooperation projects and also could not train specialist personnel on procedures and regarding their responsibilities in the event of cyber attacks (p. 24).

The Federal Council warns of a weakening of Switzerland's defence capability due to restricted possibilities for security policy cooperation and exchange, which would lead to a contradiction with armed neutrality (p. 25). Furthermore, the significant restriction of security policy cooperation could also have an impact on international armaments cooperation and call into question the reliability of Switzerland as a supplier of armaments and components (p. 25).

The initiative would indeed anchor neutrality as perpetual and armed in the Constitution, but it would restrict the scope for flexible use of neutrality. The Federal Council fears that this would lead to a rigid handling of neutrality which could no longer be adapted to new circumstances (p. 23).

The question is not directly answered in the dispatch. The dispatch states, however, that the initiative committee argues that a certain understanding of neutrality as "unrestricted" neutrality would better protect Switzerland from attacks and also represent an added value for the multilateral orientation of Swiss foreign policy and Swiss peace policy.

(p. 25) Should the preparation of a military attack become concrete, it may already be too late for efforts to cooperate with relevant alliances, as such cooperation requires time and preparation.

The initiative would no longer allow Switzerland to impose sanctions on countries that wage war.

The initiative would influence the role of Switzerland as a mediator in conflicts by explicitly anchoring and stipulating the neutrality of Switzerland in the Federal Constitution as a principle of foreign policy, and determining that Switzerland shall use its perpetual neutrality for the prevention and resolution of conflicts and make itself available as a mediator (Art. 54a para. 4 E-BV).

This would mean that the Federal Council, when shaping foreign policy, would have to weigh the neutrality as a foreign policy principle and the objectives pursued therewith against the security and foreign policy interests of Switzerland. The initiative would thus mean a stronger orientation towards the role of Switzerland as a mediator in conflicts.

However, it is to be noted that the initiative also provides for restrictions with regard to security policy cooperation with military alliances, which could possibly restrict the ability of Switzerland to act as a mediator in conflicts.

The popular initiative "For a civil status-independent individual taxation (Tax Fairness Initiative)" pursues the objectives of achieving civil status-neutral taxation and thus also abolishing the so-called marriage penalty. With the adoption of the initiative, the people and the states would make a decision on direction that obliges the legislature to specify measures for implementing the new constitutional provision.

The Federal Council's indirect counter-proposal aims to achieve civil status neutrality and thus also abolish the marriage penalty. The Federal Council has decided in favour of individual taxation, where spouses are taxed separately like unmarried partners.

The taxation of married couples under the current law (DBG) and the proposed individual taxation (E-DBG) differ in several aspects:

1. **Allocation of tax factors**: Under the current law, the tax factors (income, assets, deductions) are allocated jointly to the spouses. In contrast, individual taxation allocates these factors individually to the spouses.
2. **Joint assessment**: Under the current law, the tax returns of married couples are assessed jointly, whereas under individual taxation, each person must file their own tax return.
3. **Civil status neutrality**: The proposed individual taxation is civil status neutral, i.e., taxation occurs independently of civil status (married or not married). In contrast, the current law taxes married couples jointly.
4. **Child deduction**: Under individual taxation, the child deduction is divided equally between the parents, whereas under the current law, it is fully allocated to the parent who supports the child.
5. **Insurance deduction for the child**: Under individual taxation, the insurance deduction for the child is also divided equally between the parents, whereas under the current law, it is fully allocated to the parent who supports the child.
6. **Deduction from tax amount**: Under individual taxation, the deduction from the tax amount for children and persons in need of support is newly regulated and divided equally between the parents.
7. **Tariff structure**: The proposed individual taxation provides for a uniform tariff, whereas under the current law, a multiple tariff (married tariff, parent tariff) applies.

These changes are intended to simplify the taxation of married couples and make it civil status neutral.

The individual taxation would lead to a reduction of the tax burden on the second income for married couples, which would create an incentive for secondary earners. In particular, women would benefit from this, as they achieve the second income in most cases. The individual taxation would enable secondary earning women and men to double or triple their income without a high tax burden, which would encourage them to take up or increase their gainful employment. This would lead to a better exploitation of the domestic labour and skilled workforce potential.

The individual taxation would also strengthen the financial independence of both spouses, which would lead to better provision for old age, especially for many women, and with regard to a possible divorce (around 40% of marriages end in divorce).

The Federal Council cites several reasons for rejecting the popular initiative and instead presenting an indirect counter-proposal. These include:

1. The elimination of the marriage penalty in direct federal tax has been pending for around 40 years. With an anchoring of civil status-independent taxation at constitutional level, there would indeed be a binding direction decision for the legislator, but still measures for the implementation of the new constitutional provision.
2. The introduction of individual taxation is also possible without a provision at constitutional level and would lead to the goal faster than an anchoring in the constitution.
3. A corresponding bill was already in preparation, as the parliament commissioned the Federal Council in the legislative planning 2019–2023 to submit a proposal for the introduction of individual taxation to it.

In addition, the Federal Council states that the anchoring of the taxation method (jointly for [married] couples or individually) in the constitution would restrict the legislator.
The estimated reduced revenues from direct federal tax through the introduction of individual taxation in the tax year 2024 amount to around 1 billion francs.
The introduction of individual taxation would lead to an increase of around one third, which corresponds to an additional 1.7 million tax returns. (p. 45)

The individual taxation would lead to an adjustment of the withholding tax rates and to the deletion of previous tariff codes. In particular, this would be associated with additional expenditure for the cantonal tax administrations and the employers when introducing it. The new rates would have to be programmed, and the tax administrations would recalculate the tariff tables as a rule every year. The employers would still have to make a selection between tariff codes and clarify certain information in doing so.

The individual taxation leads to increased burdens on married couples with a 90/10 income distribution without children from a total income of the married couple of around 30,000 francs. The tariff adjustment reduces the increased burden, particularly at low and medium incomes, but cannot compensate for the increased burden caused by the system change in this constellation.

The question cannot be answered, as it refers to a statement that is not contained in the dispatch on the popular initiative "For a civil status-independent individual taxation (Tax Fairness Initiative) and on the indirect counter-proposal".
The question cannot be answered from the dispatch.

The individual taxation is to enable second earners to better plan their taxes and focus on their professional career. Women who work alongside their partner are relieved by the individual taxation, as they are no longer burdened with the joint taxation of married couples. This can enable them to work more and advance their professional career.

The individual taxation leads to the tax system hindering the taking up or expansion of a second income less. This is likely to affect women in particular, as they achieve the second income in most cases in married couples.

The more even distribution of gainful employment strengthens the financial independence of both spouses and leads to better provision for old age and with a view to possible divorce, especially for many women.

According to the dispatch on the popular initiative "For a civil status-independent individual taxation (Tax Justice Initiative)" and on the indirect counter-proposal (Federal Act on Individual Taxation) (p. 38), in the event of a separation of spouses, each person will have to fill out their own tax return. This would transfer the responsibility for the correct declaration and payment of taxes to each person themselves.

The dispatch also mentions that the appeal and remedy procedure of a spouse would not affect the legal force of the assessment of the other (p. 39). This would mean that each person would have to make their own tax return and decisions without being influenced by the decisions of their former spouse.

Overall, the separation of spouses would lead to an increase in complexity when it comes to tax returns, as each person would have to fill out and decide on their own tax return.

The position of the initiative committee and the assessment of the Federal Council on the compatibility of an import ban on foie gras with international trade obligations differ as follows:

The initiative committee considers an import ban on foie gras to be compatible with Switzerland's international obligations and argues that the highest court of the World Trade Organization (WTO) has explicitly recognized that animal protection is part of public morals. In contrast, the Federal Council considers an import ban on foie gras not to be compatible with Switzerland's international obligations and argues that the WTO legal requirements for justifying such measures are high and that introducing an import ban without prior milder measures (e.g., a declaration requirement) would likely not withstand scrutiny with great probability.

(p. 11, p. 13)

The Federal Council assumes that an import ban on foie gras and foie gras products without prior milder measures (e.g. a declaration requirement) is not proportionate and would lead to an unjustified trade restriction, which would violate GATT and the TBT Agreement (p. 13).

It also mentions that such an import ban would affect agreements with the EU and could potentially lead to trade disputes or sanctions (p. 11). Furthermore, future negotiations with international contracting parties, namely the EU, could be made more difficult.

The Federal Council also emphasizes that Switzerland, as a WTO member, is bound by GATT regulations and that an import ban without prior milder measures would not stand up (p. 13). It also mentions the TBT Agreement, which regulates technical specifications and requires that these must not be more trade-restrictive than necessary.

Overall, the Federal Council assesses the impact of adopting the foie gras initiative on international trade as negative and assumes that an import ban without prior milder measures is not proportionate and violates international obligations.

The Federal Council cites the following reasons for rejecting the popular initiative:

1. A constitutional amendment is not required to achieve the objectives of the initiative.
2. Import bans constitute serious interventions in free trade, which fundamentally violate Switzerland's WTO legal obligations and agreements with the EU (cf. section 4.4).
3. Before introducing an import ban, it would be necessary to examine, for reasons of proportionality, whether the desired objective (improvement of animal welfare) could not also be achieved with a milder measure, such as a declaration requirement.
4. The Federal Council has already initiated regulatory revisions that provide for the declaration of forced feeding of geese or ducks and could contribute to improving consumers' information about the production of foie gras and foie gras products.
5. New trade barriers would be created, which would make the current negotiations with the EU more difficult.
6. The control of imported products would be difficult, particularly since private imports would also have to be controlled at the border.

(p. 15-16)

According to the dispatch, consumers, especially in Romandie and Ticino, where foie gras is popular, would have difficulties buying these products. They could also no longer import them for private consumption. This could lead to emotional debates and tensions between the language communities of the country.

The international legal provision mentioned in connection with the import ban is the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of October 30, 1947. In the dispatch, it is mentioned that an import ban without prior milder measures (e.g. a declaration requirement) is not proportionate and would lead to an unjustified trade restriction, thereby violating GATT.

Furthermore, the Agreement of April 12, 1979, on technical barriers to trade (TBT Agreement) is also mentioned. However, in the dispatch, it is not explicitly explained how the TBT Agreement affects the rejection of the import ban.

In addition, Switzerland's obligations towards the EU under the Free Trade Agreement and the Agriculture Agreement are also mentioned. However, in the dispatch, it is not explicitly explained how these agreements affect the rejection of the import ban.

The mentioned international legal provisions are:

1. GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade)
2. TBT Agreement (Agreement on technical barriers to trade)

Source: p. 13, section "4.4 Compatibility with Switzerland's international obligations"
The popular initiative "Yes to the import ban on foie gras (foie gras initiative)" was submitted on 28 December 2023. (p. 2)
The initiative meets the requirements for validity under Article 139, paragraph 3 of the Federal Constitution. The initiative was submitted with 102,478 valid signatures (p. 6).
The Federal Council decided on 5 April 2023 to initiate a duty to declare for stuffed liver and other products (p. 10).

According to p. 5 of the dispatch, Denmark, Germany, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, and the Czech Republic are countries where beak trimming for poultry is prohibited.

The question can be answered on page (p. 9) and further in the dispatch.

The Federal Council rejects the import ban for foie gras because it is not compatible with Switzerland's international obligations and entails the risk of trade disputes. The Federal Council emphasizes that an import ban represents significant interference with free trade and would violate Switzerland's WTO legal obligations as well as the agreements with the EU.

The Federal Council also argues that the goal of the initiative committee to improve animal welfare cannot be achieved solely through an import ban. The Federal Council has already initiated regulatory revisions that provide for a declaration of forced feeding of geese or ducks and could improve the information available to consumers about the production of foie gras and foie gras products.

Overall, the Federal Council is of the opinion that an import ban on foie gras is not the best solution to improve animal welfare and therefore recommends rejecting the initiative.

The dispatch of the Federal Council states on p. 14: "Overall, it is to be assumed that an import ban on foie gras and foie gras products without prior milder measures (e.g. a declaration requirement) is not proportionate and leads to an unjustified trade restriction, thereby violating GATT and the TBT Agreement."

It becomes clear here that the Federal Council does not consider an import ban on foie gras to be compatible with international obligations if it is introduced without prior milder measures. However, the Federal Council speaks out in favour of interpreting the import ban as an expression of public morals, which could tendentially improve the initial situation in possible trade disputes.

It is therefore not correct that the Federal Council claims an import ban on foie gras to be compatible with international obligations. Instead, it emphasizes the potential consequences of such a ban and recommends rejecting the initiative.

The Federal Council rejects the import ban on foie gras and foie gras products because it believes that such a ban is not compatible with Switzerland's international obligations. It fears that this could lead to trade disputes with Switzerland's trading partners or sanctions.

In addition, the Federal Council argues that an import ban would violate Switzerland's WTO legal obligations. It believes that the import ban is not proportionate and would lead to an unjustified trade restriction.

The Federal Council instead proposes introducing a declaration requirement for foie gras in order to inform consumers about the production methods of animal products. This could contribute to reducing consumption of foie gras.

(p. 9-12)

A ban on foie gras and foie gras products could lead to problems with the EU because it could be understood as an unjustified discrimination against France due to its cultural tradition. In France, foie gras was declared a cultural heritage by the National Assembly in 2005 and thus falls under the term of "cultural traditions" according to Article 13 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Such a ban could therefore be understood as an unjustified discrimination against France due to its cultural tradition (p. 15).

The Federal Council considers the period of ten years as "short and strict" (p. 3). It is of the opinion that this period is not justifiable since it would be associated with enormous economic and social costs (p. 15). In contrast, the existing sustainability measures are better suited to finding viable solutions without the strict requirements of the initiative (p. 18).

The Federal Council assumes that the adoption of the initiative would be accompanied by a significant restriction of economic freedoms. The requirements for the economy and in particular for the primary sector (agriculture and raw material extraction) as well as the associated costs would increase with the adoption of the initiative.

The short transition period of ten years would necessitate drastic regulatory and incentive measures regarding the domestic sales market, thereby restricting economic freedom. Companies that produce for both the Swiss and foreign markets and cannot adapt their production according to the sales country would likely suffer a competitive disadvantage on the foreign market (with less stringent production requirements) due to higher costs.

The adoption of the initiative would also lead to high investments in product developments, which would be associated with financial and personnel expenses. This would primarily affect the food industry, agriculture, the construction and real estate sector, as well as the textile industry.

In addition, trade and in particular the import of goods would have to be more strongly regulated, which would worsen the competitiveness and terms of trade for economies that need these imports as intermediate products.

The positions of the Federal Council and the initiators on the implementation of planetary boundaries in the initiative differ, particularly with regard to the short period of ten years. The initiators demand that the environmental pollution caused by consumption in Switzerland does not exceed the planetary boundaries at the latest ten years after the adoption of the initiative (p. 12). The Federal Council, on the other hand, is of the opinion that this deadline would lead to disproportionate costs for society and the economy (p. 3).

The Federal Council emphasizes that the implementation of the initiative would be associated with far-reaching economic and social consequences, such as price increases, a decrease in the variety of offerings, and high social adaptation costs (p. 15). In contrast, the initiators see the implementation of the initiative as necessary to ensure the long-term preservation of natural livelihoods.

The Federal Council considers it better suited to find sustainable solutions together with the affected stakeholders than would be possible with the strict requirements of the initiative (p. 18).

The Federal Council cites several reasons for rejecting the Environmental Responsibility Initiative:

1. The initiative would be associated with enormous economic and social costs (p. 15).
2. The environmental benefit in the production country would be limited, as Switzerland's demand alone would have only a modest influence on this (p. 15).
3. The initiative would provide for a short and rigid deadline of ten years to reduce the environmental impact caused by domestic consumption (p. 16).
4. This would necessitate rigorous regulatory and incentive measures that would have far-reaching and negative economic as well as social consequences (p. 15).
5. The initiative would restrict economic freedom and reduce prosperity in Switzerland (p. 17).

The Federal Council believes it is better to maintain the existing constitutional provisions on sustainability as well as the goals and measures already set by Parliament and the Federal Council, as these allow for a pragmatic and flexible approach (p. 15).

The existing constitutional provisions on sustainability play an important role in the dispatch. The Federal Council emphasizes that these provisions already take into account today that the natural foundations of life must be protected (p. 6). It explains that Article 2, paragraphs 2 and 4, of the Federal Constitution, as well as Article 73 of the Federal Constitution, provide a constitutional basis for considering global sustainability and that these provisions already take into account today that the natural foundations of life must be protected (p. 6). The Federal Council also emphasizes that the existing constitutional provisions on sustainability are balanced and leave sufficient scope for the legislature to respond to ongoing developments (p. 8).

The Federal Council assumes that the adoption of the initiative would lead to problematic effects on society. In particular, the short transition period of ten years would necessitate strong and rapid adjustments in consumption and economy (p. 15). This could even intensify social inequalities, as employees would be threatened with job loss due to structural changes in companies (p. 16).

Furthermore, the Federal Council would expect a restriction of the freedom of choice of consumers, as prices rise and the diversity of offerings declines (p. 16). Society would also be confronted with high social adjustment costs, particularly information and transaction costs (p. 17).

The Federal Council's reasoning states: "Although the initiative aims to benefit future generations and demands a socially acceptable design, the effects on society would be problematic because the short transition period would necessitate strong and rapid adjustments in consumption and economy." (p. 15)
The initiative was submitted with 105,940 valid signatures. (p. 2)

According to page (p. 9) of the document, the Federal Act of 30 September 2022 on the objectives in climate protection, innovation and strengthening energy security (KlG), which was adopted by the voting population on 18 June 2023, contains various provisions relevant in the present context. Thus, the net zero goal 2050 for greenhouse gas emissions domestically is established (Art. 3 para. 1 KlG). The Act stipulates that all companies must have net zero emissions by 2050 at the latest (Art. 5 para. 1 KlG). Furthermore, financial assistance for the promotion of new technologies and processes is provided for (Art. 6 KlG). Finally, the central federal administration must have net zero emissions by 2040 at the latest (Art. 10 KlG).

The Federal Council's reasoning for rejecting the initiative is as follows: "However, the approach demanded by the initiators goes too far for the Federal Council; this applies in particular to the deadline of ten years mentioned in the transitional provision. In order to comply with the short and rigid deadline, Switzerland would have to take rigorous regulatory and incentive measures that would have far-reaching and negative economic as well as social consequences."

The Federal Council is thus not arguing that the initiative would proceed too slowly, but rather that it is too ambitious. It fears that implementing the initiative would be associated with enormous macroeconomic and social costs (cf. p. 15).

The question contains a misconception. The Federal Council cannot reject the initiative because it explicitly demands social compatibility at home and abroad. Rather, the Federal Council argues that the initiative would lead to disproportionate costs for society and the economy due to its short and rigid transition period of ten years (p. 13). The Federal Council emphasizes that it is committed to sustainable development that enables the satisfaction of the basic needs of all people and ensures a good quality of life everywhere in the world, both today and in the future (p. 8).

According to the dispatch (p. 16), if the initiative is accepted, it would lead to price increases and a decline in the variety of offerings, particularly for especially environmentally relevant products in areas such as nutrition, housing, mobility, and clothing.
